newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany could hit Maastricht budget target - OECD.
newsitem.headline: Germany could hit Maastricht budget target - OECD.

text.p: The OECD said on Thursday Germany could just meet the Maastricht Treaty's budget deficit criterion for the single currency in 1997 as long as it implemented all its planned austerity measures.
In its special report on Germany, the OECD forecast Germany's total public budget deficit would be 3.4 percent of gross domestic product next year -- above the 3.0 percent goal set by the treaty.
But it said this forecast only included austerity measures already achieved and not those yet to come.
"Strict implementation of all the austerity measures would be sufficient to meet the Maastricht deficit criterion," the OECD's German representative Dieter Menke told reporters.

He added, however, that the government's 1997 tax bill contained some tax cuts which if implemented would require savings measures over and above those contained in the austerity plan announced in April.

OECD official Eckard Wurzel told Reuters that the forecast of a 3.4 percent deficit in 1997 had been reduced from a prediction of 3.6 percent made in June because Bonn had achieved a very moderate pay deal for public servants for 1997.
The two officials would not be drawn on how likely they thought Germany was to meet the criterion. It's deficit rose to 3.6 percent of GDP in 1995 and is likely to be close to four percent this year.

Bonn's austerity package is designed to cut public spending by 50 billion marks and social security spending by 20 billion marks next year. Finance Minister Theo Waigel says this will be sufficient to get the deficit back to 2.5 percent of GDP.
But the OECD was not convinced: "Fiscal policy could be in danger of losing its credibility if existing policy commitments are not fully observed," its report said.

Waigel had the embarrassment last week of having to admit that the federal budget deficit -- which accounts for about half the total public deficit -- would bust its target of 60 billion marks this year.

"At the beginning of the year, reduced growth prospects pointed to a further substantial slippage from the government's budget target in 1996 and 1997 and the probability of meeting the Maastricht budget criterion appreared to be receding," the OECD said.
It said that getting the deficit under 3.0 percent would "involve difficult choices" for the government.

"Avoiding an increase in (pension and health) contributions will necessitate strict control of transfer expenditures. The Solidarity Surcharge is to be reduced and the wealth tax is to be abolished, both of which will require offsetting actions." -- Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097150
